newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union offers employers 1997 pay freeze.
newsitem.headline: German union offers employers 1997 pay freeze.

text.p: Germany's DAG trade union, which represents the country's army of white-collar workers, said on Tuesday it would be ready to accept a freeze in real wages in 1997 if accompanied by concrete job protection measures.

Speaking at a news conference in Hamburg to outline the union's wage policy for next year, DAG chief Roland Issen said the union was determined wages should at least be maintained in real terms during the 1997 wage rounds starting now.
But, with German labour relations increasingly embittered by a long-running dispute on planned cuts to sick pay, the apparent concession to employers came with a sting in its tail.

Issen said that DAG, which organised industrial action across the German banking sector last month, would continue to use all means at its disposal to defend sick pay rights, which employers may cut by 20 percent under a new law.

DAG, one of Germany's most influential unions, is involved in wage negotiations for over three million public service workers, two million retail staff and close to two million other workers in the banking, insurance and wholesale sectors.
Issen said DAG would only be looking to match 1997 wage increases with what it expects to be a 1.75 percent rise in retail prices next year, well short of previous wage demands.
Employer representatives reacted with predictable coolness to Issen's comments.

"Any wage freeze is good, but it doesn't solve the problem of itself. Several years of wage freezes are what is needed," said Juergen Stein, spokesman for the Cologne-based German commercial bank employers federation.
Wage talks for the banking sector, where most major banks have already implemented the sick pay cuts, start next Monday.
DAG's offer of a wage freeze echoes a similar move by IG Metall, the country's largest union, which is also seeking to stem the loss of jobs in the metal and engineering sectors.
A year ago, IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel was at the centre of an "Alliance for Jobs" campaign that also sought to secure job guarantees in exchange for wage moderation.
That idea ultimately collapsed when it was taken over by Bonn politicians who merged it with austerity steps unpalatable to labour.

The latest IG Metall wage freeze offer was not good enough for engineering sector employers either, who are braced for possible strikes starting next spring following the recent collapse of crisis wage talks.
Attempts to cut sick pay have caused unrest in even the most peaceable German industries, with German confectionery workers now into the second week of the first full strike on the issue.
In the chemical industry, where employers have prided themselves on their smooth relations with unions, worker protests have so far dissuaded firms such as BASF AG from implementing the law.
IG Chemie, the union representing the some 520,000 staff in the sector, repeated on Tuesday that it would be going into talks with employers on Thursday demanding that full sick pay be maintained.
